title: Character & Text Encoding
summary: Text is bytes wearing a costume. ASCII, Unicode, and UTF-8/16 are the rules for that costume, and mismatching them is one of the most common real-world bugs.

slides.subTitle: ASCII — 7 bits
slides.markdown:
**ASCII** assigns each of 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation, a handful of control codes) a number from 0-127, fitting in just **7 bits**. It fit early hardware perfectly: a byte had 8 bits, so ASCII used 7 and left 1 spare (later repurposed for parity checking or extended character sets).

It worked beautifully for English-language terminals and teletypes, and it's why `'A'` is universally `65` and `'a'` is `97` in virtually every encoding since — ASCII's layout became the common foundation everything else builds on.

slides.subTitle: One codespace for every script
slides.markdown:
ASCII has no room for accented letters, Cyrillic, Chinese, emoji — anything outside 128 codes. The 1980s-90s answer was chaos: incompatible 8-bit 'code pages', each reusing bytes 128-255 for a *different* script, so one byte meant different characters depending on which page you assumed.

**Unicode** replaced that mess with one giant codespace — over a million **code points**, each assigned to exactly one character across every script and symbol in use, including emoji. Unicode doesn't say how to store a code point as bytes — that's the job of an **encoding** like UTF-8.

slides.subTitle: Variable-width, ASCII-compatible
slides.markdown:
**UTF-8** encodes each Unicode code point as **1 to 4 bytes**, chosen so that: (1) every ASCII character encodes to exactly the same single byte it always did — old ASCII text is automatically valid UTF-8, and (2) you can find the start of a character from *any* byte in the middle of a string, no need to scan from the beginning (**self-synchronizing**).

That second property matters more than it sounds: it means byte-level string operations like 'find the next character boundary' or recovering after a corrupted byte don't require decoding the whole string from position 0.

slides.subTitle: The 1-4 byte rule
slides.markdown:
UTF-8's byte-length is encoded in the leading bits of the first byte, and every continuation byte starts with `10`:

![UTF-8's byte-length patterns: 1, 2, 3, and 4-byte sequences and their leading bit prefixes](assets/utf8-byte-rule.svg)

`0xxxxxxx` is a complete 1-byte ASCII character. `110xxxxx` starts 2 bytes; `1110xxxx` starts 3; `11110xxx` starts 4. Any byte starting `10xxxxxx` is a **continuation byte** — never a character's first — which is what makes finding boundaries from anywhere in the string possible.

slides.subTitle: UTF-8 vs UTF-16 vs UTF-32
slides.markdown:
The three Unicode Transformation Formats trade width for simplicity differently:

| | UTF-8 | UTF-16 | UTF-32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Width per code point | 1-4 bytes | 2 or 4 bytes | always 4 bytes |
| ASCII compatibility | Yes, byte-identical | No | No |
| Common use | Web, files, Linux/Unix, most new APIs | Windows APIs, Java/JS internal strings (historical) | Rare — simplicity for internal processing, wastes space |

**UTF-8 dominates the web and storage** because it's compact for English/Latin text and drops in wherever ASCII was expected. **UTF-16** persists mainly for historical reasons in Windows and some language runtimes built before UTF-8 won out.

slides.subTitle: One visible glyph, several bytes
slides.markdown:
A single thing you *see* on screen can be built from multiple Unicode code points, each of which can be multiple UTF-8 bytes:

```python
s = "e\u0301"       # 'e' + combining acute accent -> looks like 'e'
len(s)               # 2  -- two code points, not one character
s.encode("utf-8")    # b'e\xcc\x81'  -- 3 bytes total

len("family".encode("utf-8"))  # varies -- non-ASCII chars can be 2-4 bytes each
```

'Character count', 'code point count', and 'byte count' are three genuinely different numbers, and mixing them up produces off-by-N truncation and length bugs in real systems.

slides.subTitle: Counting characters by counting bytes
slides.markdown:
Truncating a UTF-8 string at a fixed **byte** offset can slice a multi-byte character in half, corrupting the string end (sometimes producing invalid UTF-8 that crashes downstream parsers) — a real bug class in database column limits and file-name truncation.

The deeper trap: even counting **code points** isn't the same as counting a user-perceived 'character' — an emoji or accented letter built from a base plus a combining mark is one **grapheme cluster** but multiple code points. "Character count" only matches user expectation if you count grapheme clusters.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: why JavaScript's string length lies
slides.subTitle: Surrogate pairs and code-unit counting
slides.markdown:
JavaScript strings are UTF-16 internally, and `.length` counts **16-bit code units**, not characters. A code point beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane (like most emoji) needs a **surrogate pair** — two 16-bit code units — to represent one character:

```js
const s = "\u{1F600}";  // one grinning-face emoji, one Unicode code point
s.length;                // 2 -- surrogate pair, not 1
[...s].length;           // 1 -- iterating by code point gets it right
s[0];                    // an unpaired surrogate, renders as broken/invalid
```

Indexing or slicing with `s[0]` or `s.slice(0, 1)` can split a surrogate pair in half, producing an invalid, unrenderable half-character — the exact same class of bug as slicing UTF-8 mid-byte-sequence, just at a different granularity. Any code that assumes `.length` equals 'number of characters a user sees' breaks the moment emoji or many non-Latin scripts enter the string.

slides.subTitle: A UTF-16/UTF-32 file's opening 2-4 bytes
slides.markdown:
UTF-16 and UTF-32 encode each code unit as multiple bytes, so a file in either encoding has to specify **which byte comes first** — the same big-endian/little-endian question that applies to any multi-byte value ([Endianness](endianness)). The **byte order mark (BOM)** is a special code point (`U+FEFF`) written as the very first bytes of the file, purely so a reader can detect the byte order by checking whether it decodes as `U+FEFF` (correct order) or the nonsensical `U+FFFE` (swapped).

UTF-8 doesn't need this — its byte sequence has only one valid order — but some tools still prepend a UTF-8 BOM anyway (mostly out of Windows tooling convention), which then shows up as three stray, invisible bytes (`EF BB BF`) at the start of the file. That's a real, recurring bug: a config or script parser that doesn't strip the BOM sees a mangled first line.
